limits: The paper develops a general decision-theoretic problem and is not a complete causal model of every hiring system.
Application to hiring remains a bounded cross-domain inference unless hiring-specific data are recovered.
observed_propositions: Observed labels can be conditioned on the historical decision policy rather than representing the full candidate population.
Selected-sample performance does not identify outcomes for rejected cases without assumptions or exploration.
sources.passage_locator: Problem statement showing that outcomes are observed only for cases selected by historical decision-makers and that evaluation on the selected sample can mislead.
sources.title: The Selective Labels Problem: Evaluating Algorithmic Predictions in the Presence of Unobservables

limits: The framework is general and does not establish the magnitude or direction of feedback in a specific hiring deployment.
No employer-specific model, response function, or drift record is recovered.
observed_propositions: Consequential predictions can alter the population and outcomes they later measure.
Deployment feedback therefore complicates claims that a model merely observes a fixed world.
sources.passage_locator: Formal treatment of prediction systems whose deployment changes the future data distribution on which the predictor is evaluated.
sources.title: Performative Prediction

limits: This is one setting and one exploration design; it does not establish a universal policy or automatic entitlement to advancement.
The study does not resolve privacy, labor, accommodation, or candidate-report obligations by itself.
observed_propositions: A pre-specified exploration policy can create outcome information for uncertain candidates who would otherwise remain unobserved.
In the studied setting, exploration improved measured diversity and hiring yield relative to the supervised policy.
sources.passage_locator: Study of 88,666 applications comparing exploitative supervised ranking with a contextual-bandit exploration policy in one Fortune 500 hiring setting.
sources.title: Hiring as Exploration

limits: The result concerns the studied vendor, employers, period, and measured recommendations.
It does not establish that every employer followed the recommendation, that every rejected applicant was qualified, or that all vendors create the same effect.
observed_propositions: A shared screening vendor can produce correlated outcomes across employers rather than independent market correction.
The study provides empirical support for cross-employer monoculture risk in the observed vendor ecosystem.
sources.passage_locator: Study summary for millions of applications screened through a common vendor, including racial disparities and repeated all-position rejection recommendations above an independence baseline.
sources.title: Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring

limits: The venue is elite professional-service hiring and should not be universalized to all employers or roles.
The research does not support moral judgments about every successful applicant or every shared interest.
observed_propositions: Cultural similarity can become an evaluative criterion and can outweigh absolute productivity in the studied firms.
The study supports one pathway by which incumbents reproduce institutionally familiar profiles.
sources.passage_locator: Ethnographic and interview evidence on evaluators using shared leisure, experiences, and self-presentation as hiring criteria in elite professional-service firms.
sources.title: Hiring as Cultural Matching: The Case of Elite Professional Service Firms

limits: Experimental results do not establish that every evaluator or employer reconstructs criteria.
The source does not identify any particular person’s motive or culpability.
observed_propositions: Merit criteria can be reconstructed after preference rather than functioning as a stable ruler.
Ex ante criterion custody is a plausible control against post hoc justification in the studied setting.
sources.passage_locator: Experimental studies in which evaluators changed the importance of credentials to fit a preferred candidate, with precommitment to criteria reducing the effect.
sources.title: Constructed Criteria: Redefining Merit to Justify Discrimination

limits: The experiments do not establish universal prevalence or a moral ranking of individual managers.
Reward-allocation findings should not be silently converted into a legal conclusion about hiring.
observed_propositions: Meritocratic framing can increase confidence and bias rather than mechanically eliminating it in the studied experiments.
Institutional self-description is not itself proof that criteria were applied neutrally.
sources.passage_locator: Three experiments testing whether explicit meritocratic framing changed reward decisions for equally performing employees.
sources.title: The Paradox of Meritocracy in Organizations

limits: Average response distortion does not imply that every applicant lies or that every high score is invalid.
The evidence does not support an individual moral judgment or a universal claim about every instrument.
observed_propositions: High-stakes applicants reported more socially desirable trait levels on average than in honest-response conditions.
Personality testing can partly reward the ability or willingness to infer and perform a desired profile.
sources.passage_locator: Meta-analysis comparing actual applicants’ high-stakes responses with honest-response conditions.
sources.publisher: International Journal of Selection and Assessment
sources.title: Faking by actual applicants on personality tests: A meta-analysis of within-subjects studies
